title: The Paradox Master
tagline: Motion is illusion — unless you can prove otherwise.

scenes.text: Elea, southern Italy, 450 BCE. Zeno is the student of Parmenides, who taught that reality is One, eternal, unchanging — and that the senses lie. Motion, plurality, change: all illusion. But how do you prove the unprovable? You construct a weapon made of logic itself.

scenes.speaker: Zeno of Elea
scenes.text: You say Achilles can outrun a tortoise? Let us think carefully. I will show you that motion is impossible — not because I believe it, but because it forces you to examine what you believe.

challenge.fact: Achilles and the Tortoise argues that before catching the tortoise, Achilles must reach its starting point — by which time it has moved. This repeats infinitely, seemingly making overtaking impossible. Calculus resolved it 2,000 years later.
challenge.instruction: Which of Zeno's paradoxes argues that the fastest runner can never overtake the slowest? Set the answer in movable type — mirrored, right to left.

scenes.text: Achilles gives the tortoise a head start. But to reach the tortoise's starting point, Achilles must first cover half the distance. Then half of the remaining half. Then half again. The sum of infinite steps — can it ever be finished?

scenes.speaker: Philosopher
scenes.text: But Achilles clearly does catch the tortoise! I can see it with my own eyes!

scenes.speaker: Zeno of Elea
scenes.text: Your eyes have lied to you before. The question is not what you see — it is whether your logic is consistent. If it cannot handle infinity, then it is your logic, not the tortoise, that needs catching.

challenge.fact: Zeno's paradoxes were a rhetorical defense of his teacher Parmenides, not his personal beliefs. He used them as reductio ad absurdum — if you accept common sense, you get contradictions. It was a philosophical weapon, not a physics claim.
challenge.instruction: Zeno of Elea personally believed that motion was impossible and that nothing in the universe actually moves. Gather what the story needs: match the goods until the tally is met.

scenes.text: Zeno's paradoxes were not solved in his lifetime. They weren't truly resolved until the 17th century, when calculus gave mathematics a way to sum infinite series. But Zeno had done something extraordinary — he forced all of Western thought to confront the nature of infinity itself.

challenge.instruction: Solve the infinite division problem — how does space halve endlessly, yet still have an end?
challenge.fact: Zeno's paradoxes were not resolved until Newton and Leibniz developed calculus in the 17th century. The infinite series 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + ... converges to 1 — Achilles catches the tortoise, and the math finally proved it.

challenge.instruction: Zeno proved — or tried to — that you can never cross a room. Solve the infinite division: how does halving space endlessly still add up to something finite?
challenge.fact: The mathematical resolution to Zeno's paradoxes came with calculus: an infinite sum of terms can converge to a finite value. The series ½ + ¼ + ⅛ + … = 1. Newton and Leibniz solved in the 1660s what Zeno posed in 450 BCE — it took 2,100 years to find the right mathematical language.
